data.title: Tesla Claims Its Full Self Driving (FSD) Saves Lives, But Wants You To Pay $99/Month…
data.description:
In 2025, an estimated 36,640 traffic fatalities were reported in the US. Let’s dig deeper into auto safety over the years and going forward.

History of seatbelts for safety

  • The first patent for a seatbelt was filed by Edward J. Claghorn in 1885, designed specifically for horse-drawn carriages.
  • Nash was the first American manufacturer to offer seatbelts as an option in 1949.
  • Three-Point Design — Nils Bohlin’s patented three-point seatbelt design in 1959 revolutionized safety, becoming standard in vehicles, starting with the 1959 Volvo. Bohlin felt morally compelled to offer his invention to all automobile manufacturers without cost.
  • All cars sold in the US were required to have seatbelts in 1968.
  • By the 1970s, many countries began enacting laws requiring seatbelt use, significantly reducing fatalities.
  • The latest seatbelts incorporate advanced features such as pretensioners, load limiters, and smart sensors, enhancing passenger safety during collisions.
  • It wasn’t enough to just have seatbelts in all cars. Wearing a seatbelt is now required by law in all US states except New Hampshire.

Air bags for automobile safety

Airbags became mandatory in all new passenger cars sold in the United States starting September 1, 1998, following the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991.

However, even though airbags save lives, they also cause injuries. A few weeks ago, my daughter was in an automobile accident where the airbags deployed. In her case, an airbag shattered her left wrist, causing a compound (bone penetrating the skin) fracture. This illustrates the potential double-edged sword of safety innovations.

The history of seatbelts shows how an innovation that was a novelty at first then became common, then when the saving of lives became apparent, seatbelt use became required.

Where do we stand on safety in the evolution of driving automation like Tesla’s Full Self Driving?

Apr 8, 2026: Elon Musk claimed that Tesla’s “Full Self–Driving” is so much safer than human drivers that it could save 90% of the roughly one million lives lost in car crashes globally.

An embarrassing personal story: On June 9, I was driving my 2018 Tesla Model 3 in Madison, Wisconsin, using Full Self Driving. At an intersection, I over-road FSD and ran a stop sign. I was struck in the rear of my car by a woman who wasn’t paying close attention and was crossing the intersection in a perpendicular way. I am certain that if I had let FSD drive the car, we would have stopped at the stop sign and the accident would have been avoided. Fortunately, my wife and I were not injured and neither was the woman driving the other car. The woman in the other car was probably saved from injury by her seatbelt.

FSD doesn’t use alcohol or drugs, it doesn’t text, and it doesn’t fall asleep. If you also speculate on how often drivers don’t pay close attention for many reasons and how often they make bad decisions while driving, it doesn’t take much speculation to imagine how often accidents could be avoided by FSD. See Waymo’s recent news as well for more on this topic.

On the other hand, there have been numerous reports of Tesla FSD causing accidents, and we don’t have full, public data on this matter.

Tesla is not only charging $99/month for its certainly lifesaving FSD technology, but it removed a potentially lifesaving technology (automatic lane centering) as a standard feature from all of its new cars a few months ago. Motivation: get more people to pay $99/month for FSD.

How is this morally defensible? Tesla has probably spent billions of dollars developing FSD up to this point. Tesla has a large team of engineers working to improve FSD and continues to train it on billions of traffic situations on a huge supercomputer. Tesla has also installed upgraded cameras and upgraded computers that enable the running of the latest version of FSD V14 in all of its new cars since mid 2023. FSD is not perfect now and it makes some sense for Tesla to have a money stream coming in so that it can continue to afford to improve it. But is this worth the price of more traffic fatalities now?

It could be quite like the seatbelt story of the past, which went from novelty to a sophisticated, proven, required feature in all cars. We are probably still in the novelty stage at this point with automatic driving systems. In fact, automatic driving systems are much more complex than seatbelts. Tesla’s proprietary FSD is arguably by far the most comprehensive, best performing automatic driving system that works everywhere in the United States today.

Tesla’s FSD is not perfect, but it doesn’t have to be. It just must be significantly safer than human drivers to save some of the now ~370,000 people who are being killed in traffic accidents in the US every year. I have been driving my 2026 Tesla Model Y with FSD V14 for 4 months now. Tesla is required to call it “FSD Supervised” because it’s not perfect. It still makes mistakes, for example, on lane selection at stoplights and with the beginning and end (parking) of trips. There is infinite speculation about when (if ever) it will be good enough to remove the “Supervised” qualifier. When will it be good enough that you can text, read a book, and go to sleep when driving? When will you be able to send your car to pick up the kids at school? Tesla has a huge team of engineers training FSD with billions of traffic situations on a huge supercomputer working to reach that next level.

However, from my experience, FSD V14 is darn good already! It has been perfect for me on the highways. I speculate that it will be good enough to eliminate the “supervised” qualification on highways in time for the next version (V15).

Have we reached the point where Tesla will be morally required to make sure that all new Teslas come with FSD as standard equipment, and will it be morally required to install the software on all Teslas that have the hardware capable of running the latest version of FSD? When will the company be morally obligated to offer FSD for free to any manufacturer willing to install the necessary hardware to run the FSD system? (Much as Nils Bohlin did with his patented 3-point seat belt design in 1959.) Tesla’s proprietary Superchargers were a huge step forward that made driving an EV cross-country practical in the US for the first time. Not many months ago, Tesla made its Superchargers available to all other manufacturers for the first time. Superchargers are now called North American Charging Standard (NACS) chargers, and they have truly become the North American standard for chargers. Are we not far from the time when FSD will be the universally adopted automatic driving standard in the US? Once again, the situation is not as simple as seatbelts. Other manufactures think that Tesla’s all-camera system will never be a good as systems employing lidar and radar as well. This will certainly be true for very bad weather. However, Tesla’s system seems much more economical to deploy and may be good enough. After all, human drivers also pull off the road in extremely bad weather.

If you find any of my articles helpful to you, please use my referral link when buying a new Tesla: https://ts.la/arthur73734 (Be sure to use it when you make your order). Tesla keeps changing the program, but here’s the latest: If you are buying a new Tesla Model 3 or Y and use my link, you will get two months of free Full Self Driving (a ~$200 value) on top of the one month that comes free with every new Model Y right now. This will get you a total of 3 months free Full Self Driving. It will be $99/month after that. For a Cybertruck, you will get $1000 off your purchase price. At this moment, Tesla is offering a year of free Supercharging with the purchase of a new Model 3 Premium or Performance.

data.title: Waymo — Nearly 1,000 Avoided Injuries
data.description:
Waymo has published another update on the safety benefits of its robotaxi service. The company says it has now logged more than 300 human lifetimes of driving, and that the safety benefits are clear already.

Across Waymo’s 270 million miles of fully autonomous driving, the company says that injuries to at least 841 people have been completely avoided. Because Waymo robotaxis drive better than human drivers (on average).

This is notable, but what caught my eye even more is that this number was up significantly from 544 avoided injuries just in December. The number of avoided human injuries has been growing exponentially, as we can see in the following chart.

Waymo provides more info: “Our latest analysis of the Waymo Driver’s safety performance now covers over 270 million miles of fully autonomous operations through the end of June 2026 — the distance equivalent of driving the length of Route 66 over 110,000 times. This safety data includes analysis of five of our major metropolitan service areas: Atlanta, Austin, Los Angeles, Phoenix, and San Francisco.

“Across these cities, the Waymo Driver continues to outperform human benchmarks. Regardless of fault, it was involved in 841 fewer injury-causing crashes — an 82% reduction compared to human drivers. When it comes to more severe collisions, the impact is even more pronounced: the Waymo Driver was involved in 95% fewer (20x fewer) serious injury or worse crashes than humans.”

An 82% reduction in injuries! And a 95% reduction for serious injuries!! That’s dramatic improvement. At this point, one could argue there should be subsidies for such service in order to protect more humans. Though, of course, it’s best of there’s a strong business case for the service and it can grow organically and exponentially.

“The safety impact extends directly to where road users are most exposed. Whether it’s riding in a bike lane alongside the vehicle, stepping into a crosswalk at dusk, or navigating dense traffic on a motorcycle, the Waymo Driver significantly reduces risk — cutting injury-causing crashes involving pedestrians by 93%, cyclists by 86%, and motorcyclists by 82%,” Waymo adds.

“View the full data and methodology here. The Waymo Driver also undergoes a formal safety review before deployment on public roads. You can see the acceptance criteria used to evaluate its readiness in this paper.”

Dive into the data if you want, and feel to share anything you notice and find important in there as well. Perhaps I’ll spend some of the weekend looking into it further myself.

data.title: How to Become Clean Energy Evangelist
data.description:
A few weeks ago, CleanTechnica published my Clean Energy Evangelist Report Card. However, 1) I left some things out which I will add here and in a future article. 2) Please see some suggestions on how YOU can be a Clean Energy Evangelist.

If you are going to be a clean energy evangelist, you need to: 1) Be knowledgeable on what’s most important, 2) Be knowledgeable on what the advantage and cost differential of each clean energy choice is, 3) Set an example by making as many clean energy choices in your life as possible. Unless you have unlimited funds, you can’t run out and reduce your fossil fuel use to zero immediately. However, when it’s time to junk your old car or if your water heater, furnace, or lawnmower quits on you, that’s the time to seriously consider a clean energy replacement. Hopefully you can eventually switch everything you own to battery electric and heat pump electric, install solar panels on your roof, and install battery storage in your garage. Also, carpool and use public transportation when you can.

A real clean energy evangelist will take his EV to car shows (see lead photo) and drives it in parades. I’ve done this for 10 years, but I was more successful in the beginning. At that time, I was able to get friends with EVs to join me. Lately I can’t get friends and family to help and I’m doing it by myself. If you look carefully, in the photo you can see my 100% Electric and 100% Automatic Driving placards on my windows. At the car show this summer, very few people were interested in my brand new 2026 Tesla Model Y. The show was populated with gas motorheads showing off their restored gasmobiles like the old red ford truck you see in the photo. I won’t do this again unless I can find someone with a more unusual EV like a Rivian truck to join me. However, I will still do the 4th of July parade.

The most important thing you can do to be a clean energy evangelist is to replace your gas vehicle with a pure battery electric vehicle. Driving a BEV is a visible statement that everyone around you will observe. If there are few EVs in your area, it’s important that people know that an EV is a practical alternative to a gas car. Seeing yours will help accomplish this. Your present gas car burns more fossil-fuel-producing CO2 (than is burned producing the electricity to run your EV that replaces it), emits more lung dangerous sub-micron particles, and produces more sub-micron particles from brake pad wear than anything else you do. A BEV doesn’t burn any fossil fuel while operating, is 90% efficient, and seldom uses its brakes. Everyone knows that my Tesla is a BEV, but when I drove another BEV brand, I had small silver 100% Electric stickers made and I put them on the front and back of the car as you see in the photo below.

sMy Tesla 2026 base Model Y rear wheel drive with mountain ebike. Pine Isle. Medicine Lake. Three Lakes, Wisconsin. August 10, 2026. Fritz Hasler photo.If you are buying a new Tesla base Model Y (see above), you can get a loan now with 1.5% interest (up from 0% thee month months ago when I bought mine) with monthly payments of ~$559. A base Model 3 got 2% interest with payments of $529/month. There is a new long-wheelbase three-row 6 seat Model YL launch edition which just became available for $992/month. With interest rates higher now, these rates are very attractive. All new Teslas have Hardware V4 that can run “Full Self Driving” V14 for $99/month. All new Teslas have an EPA battery range of over 300 miles. Those on a smaller budget can get a used Tesla for much less. A year ago, my son bought a gorgeous 7-year-old Tesla Model 3 Performance (see below) with good range and warrantee still left on the battery for $15,000.

One problem with buying a used EV is that most used car lots don’t know how to sell EVs. They don’t know what they have and don’t know how to catigorize them and communicate that information to their customers. They don’t know how much range the EV has left on the battery, whether a Tesla is dual or single motor, Tesla Hardware 2, 3 or 4. or whether it comes with a permanent Full Self Driving subscription. They don’t know if they have one of the golden few Teslas sold between mid 2023 and spring 2026 that come with HW 4 and a permanent FSD V14 subscription. Permanent FSD subscriptions are no longer available. You usually have to go to the lot and get in the car to find out this information. One advantage: Since they don’t know what they’ve got, you could possibly steal a deal.

All US EV brands can now charge at most (all newer) Tesla Superchargers, and some even have native Tesla sockets that don’t require an adapter. A Chevy Bolt EV starts at $27,600 and comes with a native NACS (Tesla) socket.

Buying an ebike is your bookend transportation action. In my case, my ebike substitutes for the second car that my wife and I no longer own. Get an ebike like the one shown above, or better yet, a mountain ebike like the ones shown below. A mountain ebike can drive on gravel if needed and can be driven off the edge of the road in an emergency. It also gives a smoother ride on any kinds of bumps in the road and can drop off and jump curbs if needed. I frequently go on errands on my ebike, especially when my wife is driving our Tesla. I pick up prescriptions, go to the gym, or pick up an item or two at the grocery store. With an ebike, you can make longer trips and climb hills much more easily. If you are not athletically able to ride a two-wheeler, an electric trike or 3-wheel recumbent bike will serve.

One thing I left out of my previous article:

  • Switch out your house to 100% LED light bulbs. Maybe most of you did this long ago, but I keep finding incandescent and fluorescent bulbs that I missed. Several years ago, I switched almost every bulb in my two houses and garage to fluorescents. More recently, when IKEA ran a fabulous special on LED bulbs, I bought 200 60-watt equivalents and threw out all the fluorescents in my Utah house, my Wisconsin house, and my Wisconsin house garage. A fluorescent bulb uses 25% of the energy of an incandescent bulb with the same light output. An LED bulb uses 10% of the energy of an incandescent bulb with the same light output. You get a double bonus here because they save you 90% of the money you used to spend on lighting…. And the LEDs last longer. They are supposed to last 20 years. I’m 86, so, in principle, I should never have to change light bulbs again. This has not been the case in practice. Maybe some of my LEDs may last 20 years, but I have had to change quite a few. When IKEA ran its 60W-equivalent LED sale years ago, I think I paid 50 cents a bulb. Unfortunately, they cost ~$2.50 at IKEA now. However, you can buy 60W-equivalent LEDs online at Amazon for $1.28 each. Saving 90% on electricity, you will pay back the installation cost very quickly, and with longer-life LEDs, this is a monetary and convenience win, win, win over time. Recently, I found a hidden 2-ft fluorescent tube bulb in a closet that had burned out. When I went to replace it, I discovered ACE Hardware no longer stocks fluorescent tube bulbs, so I came home with an LED.

I will discuss some other items in another article, e.g.:

  • Switch your fossil gas or resistance electric water heater to a heat pump water heater.
  • Switch your fossil gas furnace or resistance electric heating to heat pump heating.

If you find any of my articles helpful to you, please use my referral link when buying a new Tesla: https://ts.la/arthur73734 (Be sure to use it when you make your order). Tesla keeps changing the program, but here’s the latest: If you are buying a new Tesla Model 3 or Y and use my link, you will get two months of free Full Self Driving (a ~$200 value) on top of the one month that comes free with every new Model Y right now. This will get you a total of 3 months free Full Self Driving. It will be $99/month after that. For a Cybertruck, you will get $1000 off your purchase price. At this moment, Tesla is offering a year of free Supercharging with the purchase of a new Model 3 Premium or Performance.

data.title: Uruguay EV Sales Report: Sales Soar in August as Market Share Reaches 56%!
data.description:
Latin America’s small champion keeps making headlines and surpassing even the most optimistic expectations. Uruguay’s EV adoption has diverged from the region and reached a level that many of us would’ve though irrationally optimist only two years ago.

Amidst a booming vehicle market, Uruguay EV sales have exploded through 2026, reaching record levels in six out of the eight months this year. The result has been a market that in record time has gone from early adopter to majority adopter, going from 5% to 50% BEV market share in only two and a half years!

Let’s look at the numbers!

Market overview

EV sales in August grew by an impressive 171% YoY, getting very close to 4,000 units and even surpassing the previous records, set in July, by 22%.

Since Uruguay started providing data on PHEV sales, we’ve been able to add them to our tally, but they remain very limited, representing only around 1/10th of total EV sales. Uruguay, like most other small markets in the region, remains a highly BEV-centric one.

And now we get to the most interesting part: market share. Thanks to impressive growth, EVs now account for 56% of total vehicle sales in Uruguay, 51% of these being BEVs, meaning one in every two cars sold in Uruguay in August had a fully electric powertrain!

As a result, we’re seeing combustion-based powertrains (ICEV+HEV) melt away — despite a strong market (sales in the vehicle market grew by 16% in Jan–Aug 2026 compared to the same period in 2025), fuel-based cars have now fallen 16% throughout the year, and 20% compared to 2024.

Looking at sales per brand, the market remains balanced in August, with former uber-leader BYD still in first place, but with “only” 25% of the market, followed by Geely and GAC. It’s important to mention that Tesla is yet to start deliveries, so despite the very competitive pricing it has announces, it’s still not a part of the competition.

Model-wise, Uruguay is yet another country where the Geely Geome/EX2 has managed to win first prize, surpassing the BYD Seagull (now second) and the GAC Aion UT, a very interesting and competitive model that we seldom see on our podiums.

Year to date, BYD remains the leader, followed by Geely and Dongfeng on the podium, and then followed by GAC in fourth place and Chevrolet in fifth place. The US brand is the only legacy automaker capable of making it into the top 10 thanks to its rebranded Baojun Yep Plus Spark EUV and Wuling Starlight S Captiva EV.

Model-wise, we find BYD getting gold and silver thanks to the success of the Yuan Up (now including a PHEV version) and the Seagull, followed by the value-for-money Dongfeng Nammi. In fourth place rests the Geely EX2 (a surprisingly good result if we take into account that it only arrived in the country very recently), and in fifth place the Spark EUV.

A matter of context

Uruguay’s explosive growth in EV adoption is quite baffling. Even though there are clear economic incentives for it — mainly, the most expensive gasoline on the continent — the fact remains that fuel prices have barely grown due to Trump’s war on Iran (with only an 11–13% increase since September 2023), meaning this factor, though important, is probably not what’s driving such growth in the short term.

More important could be the announcement of new taxes for EVs from 2027: the Uruguayan government has stated it will start to charge a 5% internal tax on EVs imported at a price between USD$19,001 and $27,000, and 9% for those above $27,001. Though symbolically important, the fact is this tax remains quite low, far below what ICEVs pay (which can go up to 35%), and cheaper EVs will remain exempt.

Regardless, the announcement of taxes by itself could motivate a lot of people to jump the gun and get an EV at pre-tax prices — but since prices will not go up substantially, I doubt that we will see a significant reduction in sales in 2028. Though, growth will for sure go down. After all, you cannot sustain >100% rates of growth when you’re already above 50% market share.

But my opinion on Uruguay’s EV sales is simple: the country has found that EVs provide better value, and the population is acting on this basic fact. As time goes on, we will see this in more and more countries in the region.

Final thoughts

Uruguay’s record EV sales, and specifically BEV sales, put the country on par with global leaders, below Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Ethiopia, and Nepal, but above China(!), the Netherlands, Belgium, and the UK.

But more important than that, we’re seeing firsthand how fast things can change due mainly to EVs becoming a better option than the alternative. As a result, ICEV sales are now falling, with fleet numbers soon to follow in the coming years. Uruguay is only the first domino to fall, and soon we could see similar results all over the region.

One last thing: all this growth is happening before Tesla starts deliveries, and even if the Uruguayan market is already very competitive, we saw in Colombia that having access to a Tesla at $30,000 or less can have quite an impact.

So, what do our readers think? How long before fuel-based cars in Uruguay fall consistently below 20%? Six months? A year? Two years? Please do let us know your comments below.

data.title: Taiga Launches OS-5 Software, Bringing Industry-First Geofencing Its Electric Fleet
data.description:
MONTREAL, Canada — Taiga, a pioneering manufacturer of electric off-road vehicles and watercraft, today announced a major update to its vehicle operating system. The new software introduces a suite of advanced features, including inbuilt mapping and industry-first geofencing technology designed to radically improve rider safety and how vehicles access waterways and trails beyond the road.

Industry-First Geofencing for Safety and Access

At the core of the new OS is a revolutionary geofencing capability that gives both operators and the manufacturer unprecedented control over vehicle behavior in designated areas.

  • Custom Speed-Limited Zones: For the first time, vehicle owners and fleet managers can define custom geofenced zones where the watercraft or snowmobile will automatically govern its speed. This ensures safer operations for new riders and enables rental operators to easily draw custom zones and self-guided routes away from shorelines and potential hazards.
  • Environmental & Access Protection: To further protect access to waterways, trails and natural habitats, Taiga can work with local communities to implement manufacturer-set geofences. These automatically enforce safe, low-speed travel when riders approach sensitive ecological zones, wildlife habitats, or busy tourist areas and shorelines.

“Our mission goes beyond simply being electric; it’s fundamentally improving how riders interact with the outdoors and communities around them,” said the CTO of Taiga. “With our industry-first geofencing, we are giving owners and fleet operators an unprecedented tool to automatically manage speeds in high-traffic and sensitive zones to provide silent, zero emission and safer riding experiences.”

A Platform for the Future

Alongside geofencing, the new OS introduces inbuilt mapping, allowing riders to navigate trails and waterways with precision directly from the vehicle’s dashboard. Furthermore, this major software overhaul is designed as a foundational platform, setting the stage for continuous over-the-air updates and enhanced autonomous capabilities in the future.

The new operating system features are on display at the Monaco Yacht Show until September 26th and will be rolling out to all compatible Taiga personal watercraft and snowmobile in the coming weeks via a remote software update.

About Taiga

Taiga is a Canadian company on a mission to accelerate the transition to electric propulsion beyond the road. Taiga designs, engineers and builds all-electric snowmobiles and personal watercraft on a vertically integrated software-defined vehicle platform, delivering better access to the outdoors without compromise. Learn more at taigamotors.com.

data.title: LA Metro Secures 220 New Battery-Electric Transit Buses
data.description:
LOS ANGELES — Today, LA Metro approved the purchase of 220 battery-electric buses, one of the largest electric transit bus purchases in the country and a major step towards Metro accelerating implementation of its zero-emission bus commitment to 100% electric buses. The 220-bus purchase will more than double the number of electric buses in Metro’s fleet.

The purchase comes as Los Angeles prepares to host the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games and represents an important investment in cleaner, quieter public transportation that will benefit riders and communities long after the Games are over.

In response to today’s announcement, Sierra Club Clean Transportation for All Campaign Organizer Jennifer Cardenas released the following statement: 

“LA Metro’s approval of 220 battery-electric buses is a major win for cleaner air, healthier communities, and an electric transportation future. We applaud Metro for taking this important step toward delivering on its zero-emission bus commitment. Zero-emission transit is a smart investment as families look for cleaner, more affordable ways to get around.

“As Metro accelerates its zero-emission transition, it must ensure these investments create good, family-sustaining union jobs by upholding strong labor standards. This is the kind of progress California and the nation need to see more of.”

data.title: Glut Of Chinese Plug-In Hybrids Threatens European Automakers
data.description:
When the EU decided to put tariffs on electric cars manufactured in China two years ago, CleanTechnica contributor José Pontes pointed out that they only applied to battery electric cars. He predicted the policy would spur Chinese manufacturers to prioritize plug-in hybrids. His powers of prognostication have proven eerily prescient, as that is exactly what has happened.

According to Bloomberg, the latest report from Germany’s Dataforce shows that Chinese automakers set new records last month for sales in Europe, thanks in large part to sales of those plug-in hybrid models that do not pay a substantial import tariff. In all, Chinese brands accounted for 12 percent of all new car sales in August.

That’s pretty significant, but digging into the data makes the situation even worse for EU domestic manufacturers.

As gasoline and diesel prices spiral ever higher in Europe, new car customers are looking to lower their transportation costs as much as possible. Demand for battery and hybrid cars rose 27 percent in August, driving an increase in total sales of 4.6 percent. Without all those new plug-in hybrids and battery electric cars, the European new car market in August would have seen a significant decline in total sales.

If José Pontes saw this coming, why did the European Commission not see it as well? That is a question with no easy answer. Germany’s  Handelsblatt is reporting that the Commission is in the process of preparing a package of economic security measures that may include new tariffs on hybrids and plug-in hybrids later this year.

While Chinese cars are only about 6.4 percent of the new car market in Germany, that country is the largest new car market in Europe, so while the percentage of Chinese cars is low, the total number is significant. “Even if their market share is comparably low to other markets, the sheer size of the German market makes that move, however, very attractive,” Dataforce analyst Julian Litzinger explains.

Demand For EVs Surprises Volkswagen

Readers by now are well aware of the turmoil that changes in the marketplace are having on Volkswagen Group. Its supervisory board this year has been wrestling with how to deal with the fact that the company is making 100,000 more cars a year than its projected consumer market can support. According to Automobilwoche, the company plans to produce fewer cars at its primary factory in Wolfsburg — which only manufactures cars with internal combustion engines — and expand production of battery electric vehicles at its factories in Emden and Zwickau.

You may recall that Volkswagen was suggesting recently the Zwickau factory was superfluous and might be shuttered or converted to manufacturing weapons. But, in the past month or so, sales of electric Volkswagen cars have soared, which has forced a reconsideration of the company’s plans.

We hate to second guess CEO Oliver Blume and his compatriots, but changing long range production plans based upon short term sales data does not seem like a wise business plan.

“Demand for battery electric vehicles is noticeably increasing in Germany and other European countries,” Martin Sander, board member for sales, told Automobilwoche. He added that this marks an important “turning point in the transformation of the automotive market,” which is being driven by high prices for gasoline and diesel. It also means “lower demand for vehicles with internal combustion engines.”

Volkswagen is seeing more demand than expected for the refreshed ID.3 Neo and ID. Tiguan models, as well as its Urban Electric Car Family, which is composed of the MEB+-based ID. Polo, Cupra Raval, Škoda Epiq, and ID. Cross. All of those cars are being manufactured at factories in Spain. According to Automobilwoche, there are now more than 100,000 pre-orders for these four cars, including over 40,000 for the ID. Polo.

Such pre-orders suggest that Volkswagen is currently selling more pure electric vehicles than internal combustion engine vehicles in Germany. Increased sales are welcome, of course, but cars with batteries have a lower gross margin than conventional cars, which means many manufacturers are still under significant financial pressure, even though demand is rising. Alas, the profit per electric vehicle is still lower than for comparable internal combustion engine vehicles.

Stellantis this week said it will pause production of the electric and hybrid Fiat 500 at its Mirafiori plant in Italy for the last two weeks of October. Production of that car may only reach 60,000 units this year, Corriere della Sera newspaper reported on Wednesday. The original production target was for 100,000 examples of that model.

Balancing the interests of automakers with the interests of factory workers and customers is a nearly impossible job, but, clearly, the EU needs to do something about the flood of Chinese plug-in hybrids coming ashore. Expect that situation to be addressed muy pronto.

data.title: Netherlands Cuts 2040 Hydrogen Forecast By Almost 60%
data.description:
Three years is a long time in hydrogen strategy. The Netherlands’ 2023 National Energy System Plan projected roughly 460 petajoules of gaseous hydrogen demand in 2040. Its 2026 National Energy System Plan update cuts that central estimate to about 200 PJ, a reduction of roughly 57%. This is especially interesting as few European countries committed as broadly to the hydrogen-economy thesis as the Netherlands. Germany went further on scale, but the Dutch built policy around production, imports, pipelines, storage and manufactured demand at the same time.

The applications disappearing from the forecast are as revealing as the headline number. Hydrogen is largely gone from dispatchable electricity generation, has been pushed out of low- and medium-temperature industrial heat by direct electrification, barely appears in buildings beyond pilots, and remains only a small direct energy carrier in road transport, aviation and shipping. Much of the synthetic-fuel production previously imagined inside the Netherlands also shifts toward imports of energy-rich intermediates and finished fuels from regions with cheaper renewable electricity.

At the same time, electricity moves much more firmly to the centre of the Dutch energy system. The new plan has electricity supplying 52% of final energy by 2040, up from roughly 25% today, alongside extensive electrification of transportation, buildings and industry. That figure understates the transformation because final energy measures what reaches the customer rather than the useful work produced. Electric drivetrains waste far less energy than combustion engines, while heat pumps deliver several units of heat for each unit of purchased electricity. The Dutch plan’s own assumptions have 71% to 88% of road-transport activity electrified depending on vehicle class, about 64% of households using all-electric or hybrid heat pumps, and industrial electricity consumption rising substantially. A system with electricity at 52% of final energy can therefore have a much larger share of its actual mobility, heat and industrial work electrified.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing analysis asks what has to happen for that remaining growth to appear, what happens if it does not, and whether infrastructure planned around a much larger hydrogen future is being tested against the downside strongly enough.

The hydrogen correction looks dramatic against that increasingly electric system, but 200 PJ is still not a small Dutch hydrogen market. Current gaseous-hydrogen demand is about 130 PJ, overwhelmingly in refining, ammonia and chemicals. On a lower-heating-value basis, that is roughly 1.1 million tonnes of hydrogen per year. The revised 2040 central case is about 1.7 million tonnes, while the discarded 460 PJ vision implied roughly 3.8 million tonnes. After removing more than half of the previous forecast, the Netherlands still assumes hydrogen demand grows by about 54% from today.

The reassessment is not the product of an ideological turn against hydrogen. The economics changed as projects, financing and competing technologies provided better evidence. Earlier Dutch analyses entertained renewable hydrogen at roughly €1.70 to €4.70 per kilogram around 2030. The 2026 plan now cites bids into the first European Hydrogen Bank auction averaging about €9.80 per kilogram and Dutch 2040 estimates around €6.70 to €6.80. Those numbers make it much harder to justify using hydrogen where electricity can perform the same service directly, particularly for industrial heat, buildings, road transport and electricity generation. The plan explicitly concludes that hydrogen is too expensive to serve as either a temporary or structural alternative to electrification for low- and medium-temperature process heat. As a note, those prices are in the range I have been predicting for years, having done technoeconomic workups on projects on multiple continents to figure out if hydrogen could be both green and cheap.

That is a somewhat useful example of what technology planning looks like when comparative evidence is allowed to change the forecast. The Netherlands has not simply lowered a hydrogen target. It has removed hydrogen from applications where batteries, heat pumps, electric industrial equipment or imported industrial feedstocks increasingly make more sense. Hydrogen remains important in existing industrial chemistry and in whatever other applications can support its delivered cost, but that is a materially different proposition from an expanding hydrogen energy system spanning transport, heat, power generation and synthetic fuels.

The problem is that the Netherlands appears to have stopped the correction too early. Cutting the 2040 forecast from 460 PJ to 200 PJ looks aggressive until the remaining number is tested against the evidence in the plan itself. Current demand is only about 130 PJ, refinery output is expected to fall roughly by half, renewable ammonia increasingly loses to imports, synthetic fuels increasingly move to lower-cost production regions (reality around biofuels is lagging reality around hydrogen still), and hydrogen has already been pushed out of most heating, power generation, buildings and road transport by direct electrification. The plan also documents renewable-hydrogen costs far above those assumed when the larger hydrogen economy was conceived.

Yet after incorporating all of those downward pressures, its central case still requires hydrogen demand to grow by more than 50% from today. The NPE acknowledges that demand could fall below 200 PJ if mandates weaken, Dutch production remains expensive, electrification keeps winning or the assumed new industrial activity fails to appear, but then declines to quantify that outcome. Instead it models 200 PJ as the base case and 300 PJ as the upside. On the evidence assembled in the NPE itself, that is too timid a revision: the quantitative work cuts away most of the applications that were supposed to create hydrogen growth, then preserves the growth conclusion anyway.

That matters because the missing downside is not an academic scenario. Hydrogen infrastructure is being financed against expectations of future customers and throughput. Delayed demand can sometimes be handled by spreading early network costs over later users; permanently lower demand cannot. Once the plan’s own sector assumptions are allowed to flow through to the aggregate denominator, declining hydrogen demand becomes a scenario that deserves to be modelled explicitly, not left as an acknowledged possibility outside the quantitative analysis. The 2026 update is a major improvement on 2023, but its hydrogen forecast has not yet caught up with the evidence that produced the update in the first place.

Read the full TFIE Strategy Briefing analysis for the missing downside case, the interaction with changing EU hydrogen policy, and what lower demand could mean for infrastructure already being developed around it.

data.title: Senate Report Details Fossil Fuel Industry’s Billions in Benefits Under Trump Administration
data.description:
Washington, DC — A new report released today by Senate Democrats on the Environment and Public Works Committee puts a dollar figure on the greed and corruption of the fossil fuel industry and the Trump administration. According to the report, fossil fuel interests and affiliated groups spent an estimated $201 million supporting Trump and allied Republicans through direct contributions and advertising, along with $19 million for the presidential inaugural fund. In return, the industry has received special treatment through the hundreds of billions of dollars in tax breaks, subsidies, and regulatory rollbacks.

The report, The Billion Dollar Deal: How the Fossil Fuel Industry Bought the Trump Administration, Cashed In, and Left Americans to Pay the Price, draws on investigations into actions by the Environmental Protection Agency, the Department of Energy, and other federal agencies, as well as analyzing the finances of individual polluters.

Independent analysts cited in the report estimate that fossil fuel companies could receive approximately $190 billion in tax breaks and subsidies over the next decade from the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill. The report also highlights the administration’s rollback of federal climate and pollution protections — including the EPA’s decision to rescind the federal Endangerment Finding for power plants and vehicles — and efforts to block clean energy investments.

At the same time, the report documents the costs being shifted onto American families, including increased health costs from pollution, lost jobs from blocked clean energy investments, and increased energy prices.

In reaction, Sierra Club Director of Beyond Fossil Fuels Policy Mahyar Sorour released the following statement: 

“This report elevates a troubling reality: while fossil fuel companies throw money at politicians to fulfill polluters’ wishlists, American families are left paying for an energy system that puts corporate profits ahead of public health. We are grateful for the leadership of Senator Whitehouse and Leader Schumer who are advocating for policies that hold polluters accountable, not a system that hands them billions in giveaways while weakening the safeguards that protect our air, water, and climate. Sierra Club is calling for greater accountability for oil and gas companies and for policies that protect communities, reduce pollution, and lower energy costs. It’s time to make polluters pay.”

data.title: The Juiced Bikes Scrambler — CleanTechnica Tested
data.description:
Juiced Bikes has been one of the leaders in the long-range, durable ebikes category. Its bikes often stretch the definition of an ebike, even consistently landing in the electric moped category with motors that exceed the 750 watts typically allowed in the US for ebikes.

In 2024, Juiced Bikes declared bankruptcy, with its assets being auctioned off. After several months of uncertainty, the buyer emerged as Phoenix, Arizona-based Lectric eBikes in early 2025.

This year, Juiced Bikes is back with a revamped version of the Juiced Scrambler. It’s an electric motorcycle-style ebike that’s popular with teens across the US. It comes from the factory with a single mechanical gear and an electric motor that absolutely cranks out the power with impressive amounts of torque.

The Juiced Scrambler

Out of the box, the Scrambler is set up as a Class 2 ebike, with the motor power limited to 750 watts and the motor assist speed capped at 20 mph. You can still go faster than 20 miles per hour, but the motor won’t provide any assistance if you’re going faster. Those limits check the box on the legal paperwork — though, the Scrambler was clearly designed to far exceed those numbers.

The real power of the bike is hidden in the advanced settings where a special race mode can be unlocked that’s almost certainly the objective for any teen looking to pick up one of these. Even when you do leave it with the factory settings like we did, it’s really not ergonomically designed to pedal. The seat is a bit too wide to allow for normal pedaling for anything longer than a few seconds.

This is primarily a function of the single-speed gearing, which limits the rider’s ability to contribute via pedaling at higher speeds. The seat also doesn’t help very much, being more of a moto-inspired seat that makes pedaling awkward and a bit uncomfortable.

Having said that, it makes a great bike for teenage-sized riders to get around town on. Of course, they’ll be doing that primarily with the throttle, which is right in line with what this bike and even more broadly the Juiced Bikes brand were designed for.

The Juiced Scrambler’s rear hub motor has a peak power output of 1,764 watts and 90 Nm of torque. The high torque explains how peppy it is off the line, and I can only imagine what that feels like without the street-legal limitations on it. Race mode is clearly designed for off-road use only, but there’s nothing preventing owners from ripping around town with it enabled either.

Riding the Scrambler

We took it out and ripped around town and found the suspension and the seat to be plenty comfortable as a throttle-only cruiser.

The Scrambler takes a different approach to the display, abandoning the handlebar-mounted display common on most ebikes in favor of a frame-integrated display that sits flush in the top tube. Its colors are easy to read even in bright light — though, the small font does make it a bit challenging for older eyes or taller riders.

We found the battery life to be more than sufficient, with the majority of the movement of the bike happening with help from the battery and not my legs. The 998 watt-hour/19.2 Ah, 52 volt battery is rated for 60 miles of range per charge, and based on our testing, this seems reasonable.

If you do tend to lean into the throttle a bit more, your range will drop, with a throttle-only range per charge of around 40 miles based on our testing. Juiced Bikes also offers a dual-battery hardtail version of the Scrambler in which you should expect just under double these range numbers, but, of course, what you achieve in the real world will depend on how much of the effort comes from your legs and how much of the effort comes from the battery.

The dual suspension is plush and adjustable, which lets riders customize the comfort of the bike to their exact needs. Comfort is limited because the seat is fixed, meaning you can’t adjust it to suit taller or shorter riders.

This can be somewhat mitigated because the length of the double seat allows you to slide forward or backward to find the perfect riding position for your leg length. The double seat also means you could probably fit an additional rider on the back — though, there aren’t any pegs for the passenger’s feet to hang out on.

The Juiced Scrambler comes with a burly set of CST BFT ADV knobby 20″ × 4.5″ tires that could easily be at home on an electric motorcycle. These bulbous, knobby tires provide plenty of traction on and off road, as well as a noticeable amount of additional comfort that makes the Scrambler that much more pleasant to ride.

With all that power under the hood, it’s reassuring to know that the Scrambler comes equipped with the Talon T4 four-piston hydraulic disc brakes. Combined with the knobby tires, they provide reassuring stopping power, but the suspension can make it feel like you’re going to pitch forward if you’re coming to a sudden stop.

That’s par for the course for electric motorcycles, but it can feel a bit sudden for riders who aren’t used to the amount of speed and power a bike like this can lay down.

Overall

Everything about this bike feels premium, from the frame to the welding, to the paint, the plastic cladding, the lighting, the braking, the motor, the power, the display, and on and on. It’s an extremely well-built bike that seems like it could take years of use and abuse. Hell, this thing seems like it would smile back at you after a long day of ripping around on the track and ask for more.

The new Juiced Scrambler is backed by an impressive three-year warranty, comes with free shipping, and if their customer service is anything like the fantastic team that Lectric eBikes provides—and we believe it is—this is an extremely solid value proposition if it’s the style of e-bike you’re looking for.

That’s really the big deciding factor here. If you’re going into this looking for an ebike that you’re going to pedal around town, this probably isn’t the bike for you. But if you’re looking for something that’s going to be a great commuter platform where you’ll primarily use the throttle for power, it could be a great fit.

The real gray area on this bike is when it comes to teenagers who are assuredly the target market for this bike. Out of the box, it has a ton of power and capability, especially when you kick it up to power level 4. You have to know that whoever is going to be riding this bike can control themselves and ride it in a safe manner.

At the same time, you need to think about what would happen if and when they do unlock race mode. That can be done responsibly as part of an overall progression moving them from a traditional bike up into a more mobile platform on the path towards a larger vehicle — and, in that case, this is a perfect transitional platform.

It provides a ridiculous amount of mobility without all the registration, licensing, and insurance overhead that comes with getting an electric motorcycle. You can ride it around town and learn how to navigate with vehicles on the road while achieving a level of mobility we could only dream about when we were kids.

If you or your kids are dreaming about the Juiced Scrambler, head on over to their official website for more information or to buy one.

Specs

  • Motor: 1764W Peak Hub Motor / 750W Nominal / 90Nm of Torque
  • Battery: 52V 19.2 Ah
  • Throttle: Right thumb throttle / 20 mph max speed
  • Tires: Knobby CST BFT ADV 20×4.5 in
  • Brakes: Talon 4-Piston
  • Frame Material: 6061 Aluminum
  • Bike Weight: 85 lbs
  • Class: 1, 2, or 3 ebike
  • Suspension: KKE inverted front fork 140mm travel and KKE Rear shock
  • Pedal Assist: 4 Levels
  • Gearing: Single Speed
  • Display: Integrated TFT
  • Lights: Front Headlight Rear Tailight & Brake Light Turn Signals
  • Controller: 30-amp peak
  • Parental Lock: Set top speed between 1-28 mph locked behind 4 digit PIN
  • Sensor: Switch between Torque or Cadence
